**Narrative unity** — the unity a life has as a story — narrative identity, the narrative self, autobiographical reasoning, and the claim and counter-claim that a self is the story told of it. One of four unities kept apart (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | In relational frame theory the self is verbal behaviour's content, its process and its context, and the self as context is a perspective learned from deictic relations that cannot itself be found as content | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-060](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-060.md) | A life story constructed from adolescence on is the form a person's diachronic identity takes, and its content shapes later well-being | McAdams (2019), [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md): narrative identity is "a person's internalized and evolving story of how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", which gives a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". It arrives in adolescence and young adulthood, on the back of autobiographical memory and autobiographical reasoning, as the third layer of a psychological self after the actor of traits and the agent of goals. Stories with agentic and redemptive themes go with well-being and generativity, and in one longitudinal therapy study the story "changes first, and then the storyteller gets better". A review essay: every finding is cited, not shown, and it concedes that having a life story may be a modern cultural construction. Strawson's "Against Narrativity" ([LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md)) denies the first half for many people. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-076](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-076.md) | Diachronic self-governance is constituted by cross-temporal links of intention that are intrapersonal analogues of shared intention, not by narrative unity and not by intertemporal bargaining | Bratman (2018), [LIT-567](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-567.md): an agent governs herself over time when she is self-governing at each time along a planned activity and her intentions at those times interlock as the intentions of people acting together do, so that she acts "together" with herself. Her standpoints include a conditional, reflexive end of her own diachronic self-governance, which is what lets resolve against temptation be self-governed while following through on Kavka's toxin is not. He rejects the bargaining model (McClennen, Ainslie) in two sentences and calls narrative unity less basic in one. A philosophical model argued from cases; the analogy is partial by its author's account and its terms come from a book the record has not read. | Proposed |
